lead: A petrol engine needs a different air-fuel mixture at idle, cruise, full load and acceleration. A carburettor is a mechanical device that uses the engine's own suction to draw petrol into the incoming air and to change the ratio as operating conditions change. It matters because a mixture set for one condition is wrong for the others: too rich wastes fuel, too lean misfires or knocks. Carburettors ran millions of Indian scooters and cars before fuel injection; the same mixture-demand idea now drives electronic injection.
prereq: You need: the four-stroke SI cycle and air-fuel mixture basics from Unit 1.

blocks.text: Air-fuel ratio (A/F) is the mass of air divided by the mass of fuel entering the engine. Petrol's chemically correct (stoichiometric) ratio is about 14.7:1 by mass: 14.7 kg of air just burns 1 kg of petrol. The engine does not always want that ratio. At idle it needs about 12:1 because low air speed, poor vaporisation and leftover exhaust gas dilute the fresh charge. At cruise it needs about 15–16:1 for economy. At full load it needs about 12.5:1 to make maximum power and to cool the charge. During acceleration it needs a short extra squirt of fuel. Rich means A/F below 14.7; lean means A/F above 14.7.

blocks.where: m<sub>air</sub> is air mass flow in kg/s; m<sub>fuel</sub> is fuel mass flow in kg/s; A/F is by mass and has no unit.

blocks.text: The carburettor makes a pressure difference, called venturi depression, to lift petrol into the air stream. The incoming air passes a narrowed throat, the venturi. By Bernoulli's principle the air speeds up and its static pressure falls. The float chamber is at near-atmospheric pressure and holds petrol at a constant level using a float and needle valve. The pressure difference between the float chamber and the venturi pushes petrol through the main metering jet, a calibrated hole. A bigger jet gives more fuel for the same depression. A fixed main jet cannot satisfy all loads: at idle the air flow is too small to make useful venturi depression, so a separate idle circuit is needed. At high load the main jet alone tends to be too lean, so a power valve adds fuel. During sudden opening the fuel film lags, so an accelerator pump adds fuel. A single jet is therefore a compromise, not a complete control.
Some syllabi call the circuits idle, main, power, accelerator and choke. The table gives the role of each.

head: Circuit
Active when
Action
rows: Fuel through idle port below throttle; mixture screw sets richness
Fuel through main jet into venturi; sets cruise mixture
Extra jet opens; enriches to about 12.5:1
Squirts extra fuel; prevents flat spot
Butterfly restricts air; high depression enriches mixture

blocks.text: At small throttle openings the idle and main circuits overlap; at larger part throttle the main circuit dominates. The power/economy valve is often a vacuum-operated piston: high manifold vacuum at light load keeps it closed for economy; low vacuum at high load lets a spring open an extra jet. The accelerator pump is a plunger linked to the throttle; quick opening squirts fuel through a nozzle. The choke is a butterfly at the air inlet; closing it for cold start increases depression and enriches the mixture.

figure.caption: Required A/F by mass against load. Notice the rich idle, lean cruise and rich full-load targets; a single fixed jet cannot follow this curve.

spec.aria: A line graph of required air-fuel ratio against engine load, starting rich at idle, leaning at cruise, and becoming rich again at full load.

examples.question: An engine takes 0.045 kg/s of air. The carburettor is set for 15:1 by mass. Petrol density is 750 kg/m³. Find the fuel mass flow and the fuel volume flow.
steps: A/F = m_air ÷ m_fuel, so m_fuel = m_air ÷ (A/F).
Convert: 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³, so 4×10⁻⁶ m³/s = 4 cm³/s.
examples.answer: Fuel mass flow is 0.003 kg/s (3 g/s) and fuel volume flow is 4 cm³/s.
examples.check:
air = 0.045
af = 15.0
rho = 750.0
m_fuel = air / af
V = m_fuel / rho
print(m_fuel)
print(V)
print(V * 1e6)

traps: The main jet alone does not set the mixture at all loads; idle, power valve, accelerator pump and choke add extra fuel.
A/F is by mass, not volume. 14.7:1 is a mass ratio; vapour volume ratio is different.
Rich means low A/F (more fuel); lean means high A/F. Students often reverse these.
Venturi depression is the pressure drop at the throat, not the whole manifold vacuum. At idle the throttle plate creates vacuum but the venturi signal is weak.
The choke is for cold start only. Leaving it on washes oil from the cylinder and causes rich misfire.

quiz.q: Define air-fuel ratio and give the chemically correct value for petrol by mass.
quiz.a: A/F = mass of air ÷ mass of fuel. Chemically correct petrol is about 14.7:1 by mass.

quiz.q: Why does an SI engine need a rich mixture at idle?
quiz.a: At idle, air speed is low, fuel vaporisation is poor and residual exhaust gas dilutes the charge. A rich mixture near 12:1 keeps enough vapour to burn steadily.

quiz.q: Name the five carburettor circuits commonly listed.
quiz.a: Idle, main, power/economy, accelerator and choke.

quiz.q: An engine takes 0.030 kg/s of air and 0.002 kg/s of fuel. Find A/F and state whether it is rich or lean compared with 14.7:1.
quiz.a: A/F = 0.030 ÷ 0.002 = 15. This is slightly lean because 15 is above 14.7.

quiz.q: Explain why one fixed main jet cannot cover idle to full load.
quiz.a: At idle, air flow and venturi depression are too small to draw fuel through the main jet, so an idle circuit is needed. At high load the main jet alone is too lean for power, so a power valve adds fuel. Sudden throttle opening needs an accelerator pump because fuel lags the air. A single jet cannot provide all these changes.

quiz.q: Distinguish the power/economy valve from the accelerator pump.
quiz.a: The power valve responds to low manifold vacuum at high load and opens an extra fuel jet for steady enrichment. The accelerator pump responds to rapid throttle movement and squirts a short extra dose of fuel to cover the transient lag.

quiz.q: An engine takes 0.045 kg/s of air and runs at 12.5:1. Find the fuel mass flow.

beyond: Not for the exam. Carburettors survive in small engines, motorcycles and vintage cars, while modern small engines use throttle-body injection that follows the same mixture target. The mixture-demand curve is the same target an ECU uses when it calculates fuel from measured air flow.
